title: How We Digest Food
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Food is the body's fuel, but it cannot be used until it has been broken down into tiny molecules that can pass into the blood. This task is carried out by the digestive system, a long tube, about nine metres in length, that runs from the mouth to the anus, together with several organs that help it. The whole journey takes between one and three days, and every stage has its own task, from the cutting of food by the teeth to the final absorption of water.

Digestion begins in the mouth. The teeth cut and grind food into small pieces, and the tongue mixes it with saliva, a liquid made by glands beneath the tongue and in the cheeks. Saliva contains an enzyme that starts to break down starch, which is why a piece of bread tastes slightly sweet if it is chewed for a long time. When the food has been formed into a soft ball, it is swallowed, and the next stage of the journey begins.

The swallowed food enters the oesophagus, a muscular tube about twenty-five centimetres long that leads from the throat to the stomach. The walls of the tube contract in waves, a process called peristalsis, which pushes the food downwards. The waves are so powerful that a person can swallow while standing on his or her head, and astronauts can eat in space. A flap of tissue closes the windpipe during swallowing, to prevent food from entering the lungs.

The stomach is a stretchable bag that normally holds about one litre of food, although it can expand to hold much more. Its walls produce hydrochloric acid, which kills most of the bacteria swallowed with food, and enzymes that break down protein. The muscles of the stomach churn the food for about two to four hours until it becomes a thick liquid. The stomach protects itself from its own acid with a layer of mucus, and if this layer fails, the result may be an ulcer.

The semi-liquid food then moves to the small intestine, which is about six metres long. This is where most digestion is completed and almost all nutrients enter the blood. The liver supplies bile, which breaks fat into small drops, and the pancreas supplies enzymes that digest protein, fat and starch. The inner surface of the intestine is covered with millions of tiny finger-like projections called villi, which greatly increase its area and allow absorption to be fast and efficient.

What cannot be digested, such as fibre, passes into the large intestine, which is shorter, at about one and a half metres, but wider. Its main job is to absorb water and some minerals, so that the waste becomes solid. Trillions of bacteria live here, and many of them are helpful: they make certain vitamins and help to break down fibre. The remains are stored in the rectum until they are passed out of the body. A diet rich in fibre keeps this process working smoothly.

Digestive problems are among the most common reasons for visiting a doctor. Dr Paolo Ricci, a gastroenterologist, advises people to eat slowly, to chew well, to drink plenty of water and to include fruit, vegetables and whole grains in their meals. He also warns that antibiotics, which kill harmful bacteria, may also harm the helpful ones in the intestines, and that they should therefore be taken only when a doctor prescribes them. Good digestion, he says, is the foundation of good health. Patients who ignore persistent pain, bleeding or sudden weight loss, he adds, should see a doctor without delay, since early treatment of most digestive diseases is simple and successful.
